prompt.context: Gotham University is a university in the City of Metropolis spread across three campuses, each a ~20-minute bus/tube ride from the others. It is currently a low-ranked university. Over the past five years it has experienced declining enrolments and is currently loss-making (i.e. it operates an annual financial deficit).
prompt.question: Gotham University has asked us to help. Your task covers three areas: (1) diagnose what is driving the loss-making status and identify the most important driver; (2) using the data provided, calculate in which academic year the university will run out of its £35M cash reserves and identify which data point you would most want to verify; and (3) recommend what the university can do to fix its loss-making position and which solutions to prioritise.

clarifying_info.q: What are the main sources of revenue for the university?
clarifying_info.a: Primarily student tuition fees, with some additional revenue from sources such as cafeteria, housing, and other campus services.

clarifying_info.q: Are the three campuses all running the same programmes?
clarifying_info.a: Yes, assume they are broadly similar in their operations for this exercise.

clarifying_info.q: Has the university tried anything to arrest declining enrolments?
clarifying_info.a: Not materially. That is part of what we are advising on.

clarifying_info.q: Is the £35M cash reserve the only financial buffer available?
clarifying_info.a: Yes, assume that is the only buffer for this exercise.

exhibits.title: Gotham University Financial Data
exhibits.shows: A data table provided to the candidate with the key inputs needed to project annual cash flows from 2015/16 onwards.

framework: Structure the problem as a profitability issue: Revenue vs. Costs
Revenue drivers: number of students (volume) × fees per student (price) + ancillary revenues (cafeteria, housing, grants)
Fixed cost drivers: rent/facilities across three campuses, estate maintenance/refurbishment, central administration
Variable cost drivers: academic faculty, administrative staff scaled to student numbers
Key insight: a shrinking student base creates a dangerous fixed-cost leverage problem — revenue falls faster than costs can be cut
Market context: falling enrolment may reflect rising competition, changing student preferences, or reputation/ranking decline

questions.prompt: Q1a: What do you think could be driving the loss-making status?
questions.guidance: Structure answer into Revenue and Cost sides. Revenue: fewer students (volume decline), low/stagnant fees (price), limited ancillary revenue streams. Costs: high fixed costs across three campuses that cannot easily be reduced; variable costs (staff) that are somewhat sticky even as enrolment falls. Strong answers also note that low ranking creates a self-reinforcing cycle of declining applications.

questions.prompt: Q1b: Which of these drivers is most important?
questions.guidance: Student numbers (volume) is the most important driver. Given the high fixed-cost base (£40M/year), the university needs sufficient scale to cover fixed costs. A -15% annual decline in students means revenue falls rapidly while fixed costs remain constant, compressing margins severely. Strong answers articulate the fixed-cost leverage dynamic explicitly.

questions.prompt: Q2a: In what academic year does the university run out of cash?
questions.guidance: Build a year-by-year cash flow table starting from £35M reserves. Calculate revenue (students × fee per student), variable costs (80% of revenue), total costs (fixed + variable), annual profit/loss, and cumulative cash balance. Note the fee increase of 10% in 2017/18.

math.setup: Annual cash flow = Total Revenue − Fixed Costs − Variable Costs; Variable Costs = 80% × Total Revenue; Net cash = prior cash balance + annual profit/loss
math.answer: Gotham University runs out of cash in 2016/17, when its cumulative cash balance turns negative (−£5,040,000).

questions.prompt: Q2b: If you could check any one number from the data provided, which would you check?
questions.guidance: The best answer is the -15% annual decline in student numbers. This is the most consequential input: it drives both the revenue decline and the timeline to insolvency. If this figure is wrong (e.g., it comes from a pessimistic internal forecast vs. actual market data), the entire projection changes materially. Alternative defensible answers: the £40M fixed costs (are they truly fixed? can any be cut?) or the 80% variable cost ratio (is it really proportional to revenue?). Weak answers pick less material items like the 10% fee increase.

brainstorming.prompt: Q3a & Q3b: What can Gotham University do to fix its loss-making position, and which solutions would you prioritise?

categories.name: Increase Revenue — Grow Student Numbers
ideas: Improve university ranking and reputation to attract more applicants
Invest in marketing and student recruitment
Introduce new/differentiated programmes aligned with employer demand
Expand international student recruitment (often higher fees)
Partner with local employers for sponsored/work-integrated programmes

categories.name: Increase Revenue — Raise Fees or Add Revenue Streams
ideas: Selectively increase tuition fees (must be balanced against competitiveness)
Develop executive education and continuing professional development (CPD) programmes
Commercialise research output and IP licensing
Grow ancillary revenues: on-campus housing, catering, events, facility hire
Pursue external research grants and philanthropic fundraising

categories.name: Reduce Fixed Costs
ideas: Consolidate from three campuses to fewer (e.g., one or two) to reduce rent/facilities
Sell or lease surplus estate
Share facilities/services with other institutions
Renegotiate long-term property leases
Centralise and streamline administrative functions

categories.name: Reduce Variable Costs
ideas: Right-size teaching staff to reflect lower enrolment (but avoid over-cutting to maintain quality)
Implement shared-service models for administrative staff
Shift to online/hybrid delivery for some programmes to reduce per-student delivery cost
Outsource non-core services (IT, cleaning, catering)

categories.name: Structural / Strategic Options
ideas: Merger or acquisition by a stronger institution
Strategic partnership or affiliation with a higher-ranked university
Specialise in a niche (e.g., vocational/professional education) where competition is lower
Seek additional government or local authority funding given social/civic mission

recommendation: Gotham University must act urgently on two fronts simultaneously: it will run out of cash in 2016/17 if no action is taken.

Short-term (immediate): consolidate campuses to cut fixed costs, which are the primary structural problem given high leverage; target consolidation to two or even one campus to eliminate £10-15M+ in fixed costs.

Medium-term (within 1-2 years): invest in student recruitment and programme development to reverse the -15% enrolment decline, as growing student volume is the highest-leverage revenue lever given the fixed-cost structure.
risks: Campus consolidation may further damage reputation and accelerate enrolment decline if handled poorly
Fee increases risk reducing demand further in a competitive market
Cost cuts to teaching quality could trigger a vicious cycle of worse rankings and fewer students
Change management and staff reductions will face significant resistance
next_steps: Conduct detailed estate/facilities analysis to quantify consolidation savings and feasibility
Commission independent market research on student demand and competitor positioning
Model multiple scenarios (consolidation + recruitment investment) to identify the combination that returns the university to breakeven fastest
Develop a stakeholder communication plan for staff, students, and the local community
